questions.q: Who is the protagonist/speaker in Kamala Das's poem "Blood," and what is their relationship to the great-grandmother?
questions.a: The protagonist is the poet-speaker ("I"), the great-grandmother's great-granddaughter, who narrates the poem from childhood through adulthood. A wrong answer (e.g., "the great-grandmother is the protagonist") reveals the student confuses the central narrating consciousness with a memorable secondary character — a common error when a dominant voice like the great-grandmother's occupies significant space in the poem.

questions.q: Explain in your own words how the speaker's attitude toward the ancestral house changes from the beginning to the end of the poem.
questions.a: The speaker begins as a child who innocently promises to rebuild the house ("When I grow old... I shall rebuild the fallen walls"), but ends as an adult who abandons it ("I set forth again / For other towns") and seeks forgiveness ("I have let you down / Old house"). A wrong answer that says "she always hated the house" or "she rebuilt it" shows the student missed the crucial trajectory from childish idealism to adult compromise — the poem's emotional core.

questions.q: Apply the concept of "unreliable narrator" or "persona" to this poem: Is the speaker's childhood promise to rebuild the house sincere, performative, or something else? Support your answer with two specific lines.
questions.a: The promise is sincerely naive — a child's genuine but impossible vow ("When I grow old, I said, / And very very rich / I shall rebuild the fallen walls"). The phrase "very very rich" marks childish hyperbole, not performance. A wrong answer calling it "a lie" ignores the great-grandmother's reaction ("Touched my cheeks and smiled. / She was really simple") which validates the child's sincerity. Students often confuse adult failure with childhood insincerity.

questions.q: Analyze how the contrast between "the oldest blood in the world" (thin, clear, fine) and the blood of "the always poor" and "new-rich men" (thick as gruel, muddy as a ditch) shapes the speaker's identity crisis.
questions.a: The great-grandmother's aristocratic blood myth becomes the speaker's inherited burden: she internalizes a lineage narrative ("we had the oldest blood") that clashes with her adult reality of failure to preserve the house. The metaphorical blood imagery creates a standard she cannot meet. A wrong answer treating this as literal biology or missing the irony (the "oldest blood" produces a descendant who lets the house die) shows superficial reading of the central symbol.

questions.q: Evaluate whether the speaker's final plea ("Call me callous / Call me selfish / But do not blame my blood") is a genuine acceptance of responsibility or a deflection. Justify with evidence from the poem's closing imagery.
questions.a: It is both: she admits fault ("I have let you down," "I seek forgiveness") but frames her failure as inevitable — her "thin, clear, fine" blood "remembers as it flows" the past glory but cannot act on it. The blood becomes a metaphor for inherited privilege without power. A wrong answer calling it purely "selfish excuse" or "noble acceptance" misses the poem's deliberate ambiguity — the hallmark of Das's confessional mode.

questions.q: Create a four-line stanza in free verse that captures the speaker's voice ten years after the poem ends, showing whether she has made peace with her choice or not.
questions.a: A strong response mirrors the poem's imagery (rats, white ants, Arabian Sea) and tonal complexity (guilt + resignation). Example: "The mango smoke still stains my dreams at night / No renovation grants the dead their due / I visit now in verses, not in brick / The oldest blood runs thin — but runs true." A weak answer uses generic regret without the poem's specific symbols or the speaker's distinctive voice.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: Character analysis of the protagonist in a poem involves identifying the speaker/persona, tracing their perspective shifts across the poem, and explaining how their voice, memories, and conflicts reveal their personality and thematic ______ — all supported by specific textual evidence.
Fill in the blank: Imagine you're listening to a grandparent recount family ______ — you hear pride, nostalgia, and perhaps regret in their voice.
What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: The student can independently identify the speaker's traits at different life stages, trace the evolution of their relationship with the ancestral house and great-grandmother, and write a structured PEEL-response using at least three pieces of textual evidence to support their analysis.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: Imagine you're listening to a ______ recount family history — you hear pride, nostalgia, and perhaps regret in their voice.
